This is IntelliRoute: dynamic network routing, and multi-criteria path optimization.
We will build it with classical algorithms, graph theory, and mathematical optimization.
And we will understand it from scratch, so that when the professor asks, we can explain every line.
First: what is routing? When your computer sends a message to a server, it does not travel directly.
It hops through devices called routers. Each router receives the packet, and decides where to forward it next.
Three words to remember. A router forwards packets. A link connects two routers. A packet is a small unit of data.
Think of routers as cities, links as roads, and packets as cars.
Routing is simply deciding which roads the data should take.
Now, the real problem. A packet must travel from router A to router F, and there are several possible paths.
The obvious choice is the shortest one. But the shortest route is not always the fastest, or the most reliable.
One path has three links, but one of them is heavily congested. Another has four links, all fast. A third has only two, but it loses packets.
So which path is best? That depends on what we want to optimize.
Our research question: how can we dynamically select the most efficient route, using several performance parameters, instead of the shortest path alone?
Our foundation is Dijkstra's algorithm, developed by Edsger Dijkstra in nineteen fifty-six.
Its job is simple: find the path with the lowest total cost, between a start node and a destination.
Take this small network. Each number is the cost of crossing a link. We want to go from A to F.
Through B and D, the cost is eleven. Through B and E, fourteen. Through C and E, only seven. So the best path is A, C, E, F.
But Dijkstra does not list every path. It starts at A with distance zero, and looks at its neighbours: B costs four, C costs two.
Then it always picks the unvisited node with the smallest known cost, and updates its neighbours. This update is called relaxation.
The result is guaranteed optimal, as long as no weight is negative.
Here is the limitation. Suppose congestion raises the link from A to C, from two, to fifteen.
The old route is no longer optimal. Dijkstra can find the new one, but only if someone updates the weights and runs it again.
It does not monitor the network, and it does not decide how to model it. That is where our project begins.
Our idea: give every link a cost built from several measurements. Latency, packet loss, available bandwidth, and congestion.
The weights of this formula express what we want to optimize, and the costs are refreshed as conditions change.
To avoid switching routes too often, the system only changes path when the gain is significant.
What will we build? Not real internet routers. A network simulator, written in Python.
Part A: a topology editor, to create routers, connect them, and choose a source and a destination.
Part B: a condition simulator, to add congestion, latency, packet loss, and even router failures.
Part C: the routing engine, with three strategies. Static Dijkstra, Dijkstra with updated weights, and our multi-criteria adaptive routing.
Part D: a results dashboard, showing the selected route, its cost, the latency, the delivery ratio, and the route changes.
How do we prove that it is better? With experiments, not with adjectives.
We run one hundred simulated scenarios, and compare the algorithms under identical conditions.
We measure average latency, packet delivery ratio, throughput, computation time, and the number of route changes.
And we keep the comparison honest. We also test against Dijkstra using updated latency weights, to see whether multiple criteria really add value.
Now, who does what? Three teammates, plus an AI assistant.
Member one leads the algorithms: the graph model, both Dijkstra baselines, and the multi-criteria cost function.
Member two leads the simulator: the topology editor, the network conditions, and the dashboard.
Member three leads the experiments and the report: scenarios, metrics, plots, and the LaTeX document.
The AI drafts code skeletons, tests, LaTeX, and diagrams, and it explains concepts. It is fast, but it can be confidently wrong, and it cannot see our real results.
So every AI output has a human owner, who checks it, and can explain it without notes.
Humans own the research question, the experiments, and every final claim.
The final report is written in LaTeX, with the algorithms, the model, the experiments, and this plan.
IntelliRoute. Not just the shortest path. The best one, for the conditions right now.
